name: creduce
desc: Reduce a C/C++ program while keeping a property of interest
why: Automatically shrinks a crashing C program to a minimal case, a fascinating look at test-case reduction, though deprecated.

brief.what_it_is: C-Reduce is a command-line tool for shrinking C or C++ source files. You give it a large program and a test script (the interestingness test) that says whether the program still has some property, such as triggering a compiler bug. It repeatedly tries smaller variants and keeps the ones that still pass the test, and it outputs a much smaller C/C++ program with the same property. The README says it also reduces programs in other languages such as JavaScript and Rust, though it is built for C/C++.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it is intended for people who discover and report bugs in compilers and other tools that process C/C++ code, who need a minimal test case to report.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes the reduction loop only briefly: it searches for smaller versions of the input that keep the property of interest. Each run of the interestingness test happens in a fresh temporary directory containing a copy of the file being reduced. With more than one core it runs candidate compiler invocations in parallel and may kill them when they are no longer useful. The README does not explain the reduction passes in detail; INSTALL.md mentions an internal clang_delta tool built against LLVM/Clang.

brief.install_notes: INSTALL.md says to try a package manager first (brew, apt, and others). A source build needs Perl, C++ and C toolchains, Flex, zlib, and LLVM/Clang 9.0.0 (a pre-built binary package is enough; no need to compile LLVM). Perl modules needed are Exporter::Lite, File::Which, Getopt::Tabular and Regexp::Common; Term::ReadKey is optional. Build with configure and make, or with CMake, and build with clang++ if you hit C++ link errors. The master branch needs specific LLVM versions; a llvm-svn-compatible branch exists for newer LLVM. The README gives no first-run configuration.
brief.standout: Its own README says it does a good job on languages other than C/C++, such as JavaScript and Rust, which is an unusual claim for a tool built around C. The design choice of running each interestingness test in a fresh temporary directory keeps the test script simple.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release date or deprecation notice. The INSTALL.md pins LLVM/Clang 9.0.0 and FreeBSD 12.1, which suggests the install docs have not been updated in a long time, but I could not confirm the last commit or release date from the pages I fetched. The scout note calls the project deprecated, which I could not verify from the README.
brief.caveats: The README warns that using more than one core can leak space in /tmp when compilers are killed mid-run, with suggested workarounds (--n 1, -pipe, TMPDIR). Source builds need Perl modules, Flex, zlib, and specific LLVM/Clang versions, and GNU Make specifically. GCC 5.x had link-time problems, so the docs recommend clang++. Your interestingness test must copy in or use absolute paths for any extra files it needs. The web page link in the README (embed.cs.utah.edu/creduce) did not return C-Reduce content when I fetched it, so the project docs could not be checked directly. The scout note's 'deprecated' label is not backed by the README I read.

entry.title: C-Reduce
entry.tldr: Give it a huge C or C++ file and a test script, and it shrinks the file to a tiny program that still does the same thing.
entry.deeper_look:
C-Reduce takes a large C or C++ program that has some property of interest, such as triggering a compiler bug, and automatically produces a much smaller program with the same property. You supply the property as an "interestingness test", a script that exits successfully when the file still shows the behaviour. The tool tries smaller variants, keeps the ones that still pass, and repeats.

It exists for people who find and report bugs in compilers and other tools that process C/C++. A bug report that says "this 20,000-line file crashes the compiler" is hard to act on. A ten-line file is easy. Doing that shrinking by hand is tedious, so C-Reduce does it for you.

The idea underneath is test-case reduction: define a property as a yes/no question, then search for the smallest input that still answers yes. The README does not detail the reduction passes, but INSTALL.md mentions an internal tool, clang_delta, built against LLVM/Clang. Each run of your test happens in a fresh temporary directory holding a copy of the file being reduced, which keeps test scripts simple.

The README also says it does a pretty good job on languages other than C/C++, such as JavaScript and Rust, even though it was built for C.
entry.install:
brew install creduce
# Homebrew pulls in astyle and llvm@21 as dependencies. You also need your own interestingness test script.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the options and shows how to pass in your interestingness test and the file to reduce.
Runs on a single core so it never kills a running compiler instance, which avoids leaking files into /tmp. Add your test script and source file as arguments.

entry.whats_unique: It turns "make this bug report smaller" into an automated search driven by a script you write. Its README also claims it handles JavaScript and Rust reasonably well despite being built around C.
entry.caveats: Homebrew marks the formula deprecated, though the README I read does not say so, and the install docs pin old LLVM and FreeBSD versions. The README also warns that running on more than one core can leak space in /tmp.
